The most common box in the world. A steel box the size of a small room, about as long as a small truck.
10 standard (1.2 × 1.0 m) or 11 Euro (1.2 × 0.8 m) pallets
Heavy, compact cargo: tiles, granite, rice, sugar, metal parts, machinery, chemicals in drums or bags.
It fills up by weight before it fills up by space. Road weight limits in India and at destination may stop you from loading the full payload.
Floor tested for a forklift axle of 7,260 kg. Rule of thumb: keep heavy items to about 4.5 tonnes per running metre of floor.
Twice as long as a 20′ but it cannot carry twice the weight. Best when your cargo is bulky rather than heavy.
Light or medium cargo that takes up space: furniture, garments, handicrafts, cartons of consumer goods.
Same maximum weight as a 20′ (about 30.5 tonnes in total), so it can actually carry slightly less cargo by weight.
Floor tested for a forklift axle of 7,260 kg. Rule of thumb: about 3 tonnes per running metre. Spread heavy items along the length.
A 40′ that is one foot (30 cm) taller. The extra height gives about 13% more space for the same footprint.
21 standard or 25 Euro pallets, with more room to stack
Bulky, light cargo and anything tall: cotton, foam, furniture, garments on hangers, cartons stacked high.
Taller boxes can hit height limits on some roads and rail routes. Look for the yellow and black stripes that mark a high cube.
Floor tested for a forklift axle of 7,260 kg. Rule of thumb: about 3 tonnes per running metre.
The longest standard box, 5 feet longer than a 40′ high cube. Less common in India.
Very light, bulky cargo where every cubic metre counts.
Not every line, port or trailer handles 45′ boxes. Ask us before planning around one.
A fridge on the move. It has its own cooling unit at one end and keeps a set temperature, usually from −30 °C to +30 °C.
Frozen or chilled food, fruit and vegetables, pharmaceuticals, chemicals that must stay cool.
Thick insulated walls mean less space inside than a normal 20′. It needs power at the port and on the ship, which adds cost.
T-shaped floor lets cold air flow under the cargo. Do not block the air flow and do not load above the red line.
The standard long reefer. Most 40′ reefers today are high cubes.
Larger volumes of chilled or frozen cargo: fruit, meat, seafood, dairy, vaccines and medicines.
Pre-cool the cargo before loading. A reefer keeps cargo cold; it is not designed to cool warm cargo down.
T-shaped floor for air flow. Keep cargo below the red load line and leave space at the door end.
A 20′ with no hard roof, just a removable tarpaulin, so cargo can be lowered in from above by crane.
Tall or heavy items that cannot go through the doors: machinery, marble blocks, pipes, cable drums.
Cargo taller than the walls is 'out of gauge' and costs more. Fewer of these boxes are available, so book early.
Strong floor for heavy machinery, but spread the load. Lashing rings inside for securing cargo.
In gauge or out of gauge?
Cargo fits completely inside the walls and below the top edge (inside height about 2.35 m). The tarpaulin closes over it and it is priced like a normal open top.

Cargo taller than the walls is 'out of gauge' (over-height). The tarpaulin cannot close, nothing can be stacked on top of it on the ship, and the line charges extra for the space it blocks. It needs the shipping line's approval before booking.
Send us the exact length, width, height and weight of each piece, ideally with a drawing, and we will tell you if it fits in gauge.
The long version of the open top, for long items that must be loaded from above.
Long pipes, steel structures, timber, long machinery parts.
Tarpaulin roof is not watertight like a steel roof. Protect sensitive cargo.
Rule of thumb: about 3 tonnes per running metre. Lashing rings along the sides.
A strong floor with two end walls and no sides or roof. Cargo can stick out of the sides or top.
Very heavy or oversized items: generators, transformers, vehicles, boats, construction machines.
Cargo wider or taller than the rack is 'out of gauge' and needs special stowage and pricing. Must be lashed properly.
Heavy-duty floor built for concentrated weight, but load must still be spread and secured to the lashing points.

Cargo stays within the outline of a normal container: no wider than the rack (2.44 m outside) and no taller than a standard container (2.59 m including the rack floor). It is handled almost like a normal box.

Cargo that is wider (over-width), taller (over-height) or longer (over-length) than that outline is 'out of gauge'. It takes up space next to or above it on the ship, so the line charges for those lost slots, and it may need special road permits or escorts in India.
For out-of-gauge cargo we need exact dimensions, weight, centre of gravity and lifting points before the line will accept the booking. Ask us early.
The long flat rack. It can carry up to about 40 tonnes, far more than a normal 40′.
Long and very heavy cargo: industrial machinery, boilers, heavy vehicles, large steel structures.
Check road permits for heavy and wide loads in India and at destination before you book.
Built for heavy concentrated loads. Ask us for a lashing and weight distribution plan.
A steel tank inside a container-sized frame, for liquids in bulk instead of drums.
Liquid chemicals, oils, food-grade liquids, some hazardous liquids.
Must be filled between about 80% and 95% to stop the liquid surging, so the real cargo weight depends on the tank size and how heavy the liquid is. Cleaning certificates are needed between loads.
No floor: the load sits in the tank. The frame stacks like any other container.

Can I really load 28 tonnes into a 20 foot container?

The container can take it, but the road often cannot. Truck weight limits in India and in the destination country may cap what you can carry on the road leg. Tell us your route and we will tell you the safe maximum.
What is the difference between a 40′ and a 40′ high cube?

Same length and width, but the high cube is 30 cm taller inside. That gives about 9 m³ more space. The price difference is usually small, so for light, bulky cargo the high cube is often the better deal.
How much cargo really fits in a container?

Less than the full volume, because cartons never fit perfectly and you need space to load. Plan on about 25–28 m³ in a 20′, 55–58 m³ in a 40′ and 65–68 m³ in a 40′ high cube. Our container load calculator can work it out from your packing list.
Where can I see the exact weights of my container?

On the CSC safety plate and the markings on the container door. They show the exact empty weight (tare) and maximum gross weight for that particular box, which can differ slightly from the typical figures here.
Verified Gross Mass: the total weight of the container including cargo, packing and the container itself. It must be declared to the shipping line before the container is loaded on the ship.

Heavy, dense cargo usually goes in a 20′. Light, bulky cargo goes in a 40′ or 40′ high cube. Temperature-sensitive goods need a reefer, and oversized or very heavy items need an open top or flat rack. WhatsApp us your packing list and we will suggest the best fit.
